tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: ShareOnboardingGuide
tools.description:
Upload the ONBOARDING.md in the current directory and return a share link teammates can open in Claude Code. Call this after the user has confirmed the final content.

When called with the default mode='check': if a local ONBOARDING.md is present, uploads it to the most-recently-updated org guide (or creates one if none exist) and returns a fresh link. If no local file is present, returns the existing link without uploading (status: has_existing).

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestSkills
tools.description:
Render a card of standalone skills the user can add — org, shared, or Anthropic skills not yet enabled.

Call this when the task is one a skill could make repeatable — drafting in a house style, reviews against a playbook, a recurring workflow — and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about skills. Also when they ask for recommendations, or when ListSkills returned zero matches. Use ListSkills for skills they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a skill would help, or if you already rendered a suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Pass keywords drawn from the task itself, and set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find).

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size stays on that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane) until you call this tool again with preset "desktop", so reset it once you are done testing. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent, 5 touch points, and mouse-to-touch translation (hover stops producing hover states). Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

## 1. Goal statement

**Changes** — all in `overrides/app/utils/`:

**`regionPrefCookie.ts`** — contract, spec only what's specified:
```
zimm-region-pref=1|l=<epochSeconds>|c=<epochSeconds>
path=/; samesite=lax; secure; max-age=<long>
```
`l` = language prompt dismissed/acted, `c` = country prompt. **No `s` flag** — nothing specifies storing a manual selection; the `1|` version prefix means adding one later strands nothing. Exports a named `LANGUAGE_PROMPT_SUPPRESSION_DAYS = 7` constant. **Parse and serialise must be pure and isomorphic** (zero `document` reference), with thin client `get`/`set` on top — the client writes it and the server will later read it from the `Cookie` header in `request-processor.js`. One module, four eventual consumers (689, 823, 688, 817); otherwise 817 re-implements the parser and the two drift. `try/catch` on **read and write** (Safari private mode throws on *read* — see `useRecentlyViewedHistory.ts:30`), plus an SSR guard (`typeof document === 'undefined'`). Not `httpOnly`.

**`crossSiteUrl.ts`** — strip the base path and the current site alias, then `buildUrl(path, targetAlias, targetLocale)`. `getPathWithLocale` cannot be reused: it swaps the locale *within one site*, and the four EU languages are separate **sites**. **`shouldShowLanguagePrompt.ts`** — pure predicate:
```ts
shouldShowLanguagePrompt({ sfccSiteId, currentLanguage, browserLanguages, suppressedAt, now })
  : { show: boolean; targetLanguage?: string }
```
Gate is `sfccSiteId === 'ZimmermannEU'` — one comparison covering all four EU domestic PWA sites and naturally excluding EU International (`ZimmermannEUIntl`, English-only). **Match on the primary subtag, both sides**: browsers report `fr-FR`, `it-CH`, `en-AU`; our site locales are `fr`, `it`, `es`, `en-GB`. `fr-FR`→`fr` and our `en-GB`→`en`, or a French shopper reporting `fr-FR` never matches and the prompt silently never fires. Read-time window enforcement, not browser expiry.

### Step C1 — three pure helpers *(no dependency on A or B — parallelisable)*

**Changes** — all in `overrides/app/utils/`:

**`regionPrefCookie.ts`** — contract, spec only what's specified:

```
zimm-region-pref=1|l=<epochSeconds>|c=<epochSeconds>
path=/; samesite=lax; secure; max-age=<long>
```

`l` = language prompt dismissed/acted, `c` = country prompt. **No `s` flag** — nothing specifies
storing a manual selection; the `1|` version prefix means adding one later strands nothing. Exports
a named `LANGUAGE_PROMPT_SUPPRESSION_DAYS = 7` constant. **Parse and serialise must be pure and
isomorphic** (zero `document` reference), with thin client `get`/`set` on top — the client writes it
and the server will later read it from the `Cookie` header in `request-processor.js`. One module,
four eventual consumers (689, 823, 688, 817); otherwise 817 re-implements the parser and the two
drift. `try/catch` on **read and write** (Safari private mode throws on *read* — see
`useRecentlyViewedHistory.ts:30`), plus an SSR guard (`typeof document === 'undefined'`). Not
`httpOnly`.

**`crossSiteUrl.ts`** — strip the base path and the current site alias, then
`buildUrl(path, targetAlias, targetLocale)`. `getPathWithLocale` cannot be reused: it swaps the
locale *within one site*, and the four EU languages are separate **sites**. Preserve the path, drop
`refine` (`disallowParams: ['refine']`), matching `footer/index.jsx:152`. Returns a string; the
caller performs the hard navigation.

**`shouldShowLanguagePrompt.ts`** — pure predicate:

```ts
shouldShowLanguagePrompt({ sfccSiteId, currentLanguage, browserLanguages, suppressedAt, now })
  : { show: boolean; targetLanguage?: string }
```

Gate is `sfccSiteId === 'ZimmermannEU'` — one comparison covering all four EU domestic PWA sites and
naturally excluding EU International (`ZimmermannEUIntl`, English-only). **Match on the primary
subtag, both sides**: browsers report `fr-FR`, `it-CH`, `en-AU`; our site locales are `fr`, `it`,
`es`, `en-GB`. `fr-FR`→`fr` and our `en-GB`→`en`, or a French shopper reporting `fr-FR` never
matches and the prompt silently never fires. Read-time window enforcement, not browser expiry.

Plus a `.test.ts` beside each.

- [ ] `shouldShowLanguagePrompt` tests cover all six branches: non-EU site → false; EU site, browser language matches URL → false; EU site, browser language differs and is one of the four → true with the right target; EU site, browser language is none of the four → false; within suppression window → false; window lapsed → true. Plus the primary-subtag cases `fr-FR`→`fr` and `en-GB`→`en`.
- [ ] Pure functions, no side effects, no imports from `overrides/app/hooks/` (utilities must not depend on hooks — the dependency runs the other way).

**Mandatory sub-step — prove each test can fail.** Three new test files. For each, invert at least
two assertions, confirm red, revert. The window-lapsed and primary-subtag cases specifically: those
are the two that would pass trivially against a stub.

**Loop config**

| Agent | Weight | Brief |
|---|---|---|
| Tester | **Heavy** | Run all six predicate branches explicitly. Run both Safari-private-mode throw paths (read and write) — a `try/catch` nobody exercised is a `try/catch` nobody wrote correctly. Capture fail-on-purpose reds. |
| Scope-check | Light | Six new files, all Tier 4. `package.json`/`package-lock.json` untouched. No hook imports. |
| Scorer | PASS when | tsc clean **and** 81 files / 0 failures **and** zero `js-cookie` references **and** zero `document` references in the pure half **and** all six branches covered **and** documented red-then-green inversions. |

---

### Step C2 — `useCountryConfig` defect fix

**This is the one step that can be dropped without affecting either story's ACs.** SFCC-689's own
gate reads `sfccSiteId` directly and does not call this hook. It is here because it is the obvious
hook to reach for, and reaching for it silently gives you Australia.

**Changes**

- `overrides/app/hooks/useCountryConfig.ts`: the match is `c.sfccSiteId === site?.id` — the config's
  SFCC id (`ZimmermannEU`) compared against the runtime's PWA site id (`ZimmermannEUfr`). It never
  matches on any of the four EU domestic sites, so it silently returns the **AU** config. One-line
  fix: `site?.sfccSiteId ?? site?.id`. Confirmed safe — `config/sites.js:31` emits `sfccSiteId`
  **only** for the four EU domestic sites (`...(sfccSiteId ? { sfccSiteId } : {})`), so the `??`
  fallback is exercised on the other six and behaviour there is byte-identical.
- `overrides/app/hooks/useCountryConfig.test.ts`: the existing suite mocks `site.id` as
  `'ZimmermannEU'` — a value `config/sites.js` **can never emit**. The test passes and the runtime
  fails. Correct the mocks to the real shape.
- `overrides/app/components/footer/index.tsx` ~line 195 — **Tier 2, comment-only.** The comment
  currently cites this exact bug as verified precedent: *"confirmed against useCountryConfig.ts's
  identical client-side pattern (`c.sfccSiteId === site?.id`), the existing precedent for this exact
  lookup."* Leaving it propagates the defect as a house pattern. Reword only; **no code change in
  this file.**

**Pass criteria**

- [ ] `npx tsc --noEmit` → exit 0.
- [ ] `npm run test` → 0 failures; `useCountryConfig.test.ts` still reports **11 tests** or more.
- [ ] **Fail-on-purpose is mandatory and is the whole point here.** Before the fix: add a test asserting `ZimmermannEUfr` + locale `fr` resolves to the France config, and confirm it goes **red** against the current implementation. Then apply the one-line fix and confirm green. A test suite that passed for months against an impossible mock value is exactly the case where a green run proves nothing.
- [ ] `git diff overrides/app/components/footer/index.tsx` shows **comment lines only** — no executable line changed. Verify with `git diff -U0` and read it.
- [ ] Grep confirms no remaining `c.sfccSiteId === site?.id` anywhere.

**Loop config**

| Agent | Weight | Brief |
|---|---|---|
| Tester | Medium | The new EU-site assertion must be demonstrated red-before-green. Confirm all six non-EU sites still resolve identically (regression, not just the fix). |
| Scope-check | **Heavy** | `footer/index.tsx` is Tier 2. Prove the diff is comment-only. If a single executable line moved, stop and re-scope. |
| Scorer | PASS when | tsc clean **and** suite green **and** a captured red-then-green for the EU case **and** `footer/index.tsx` diff is provably comment-only. |

---

### Step C3 — mount the prompt in `_app` *(the sharpest review point)*

**Changes**

1. **ADD** `overrides/app/components/ui-kits/organisms/zimmLanguagePrompt/index.tsx` — the
   container. Takes `{ site, locale, buildUrl }` **as props** (`_app` already destructures all three
   from `useMultiSite()` at `index.tsx:172`). Owns one `useState` (`isOpen`) and one client-only
   `useEffect` that reads `navigator.languages` and the suppression cookie, calls
   `shouldShowLanguagePrompt`, and opens. Renders `ZimmCountryLanguageMismatch variant="language"`
   or `null`.

   **Props, not its own `useMultiSite` call.** The handbook allows only `useIntl` and `useUiCopy` as
   hook exceptions inside `components/`; passing the three values it already has from the Tier 2
   parent keeps the container unambiguously prop-driven and keeps the `_app` diff to three lines.

   **Cookie first, then navigate.** `window.location =` unloads the page; an async write may never
   land. Hard navigation, not client-side routing — switching site changes the Commerce API
   `siteId`, the basket context and the locale, all resolved from the URL at boot. A route change
   would update the address bar and leave the app on the old site's API.

2. **ADD** its `index.stories.tsx` (two thin stories: eligible, suppressed — no `play`; the
   interaction assertions live on B1's story) and `index.test.tsx`.
3. **MODIFY** `overrides/app/components/_app/index.tsx` — **Tier 2.** One import plus one JSX
   element with three props, mounted alongside the existing `<AuthModal {...authModal} />` at
   ~line 482. Nothing else.
4. **MODIFY** `overrides/app/components/_app/index.test.tsx` — **Tier 2.** One `vi.mock` of the new
   container, plus one new positive assertion.

**Why the test file must change, stated plainly for the PR body:** `_app/index.test.tsx` exists
specifically to assert that a global modal never renders again — SFCC-863 removed Salesforce's DNT
placeholder and left a regression suite behind. This PR adds a *different* global modal, which is
legitimate but looks exactly like the thing that suite forbids. Two facts settle it:

- The suite asserts on **`DntNotification` specifically**, by spy and by `data-testid`, not on "no modal renders". Adding an unrelated modal cannot make it fail on its own terms.
- The existing `use-multi-site` mock at `_app/index.test.tsx` returns `site: { id: 'ZimmermannAU' }` with **no `sfccSiteId` field**, so the new gate evaluates `undefined === 'ZimmermannEU'` → false → the prompt renders `null` in that suite regardless.

The mock is needed purely because of the module-eval `ZimmIcon` throw described in the manifest, not
because the prompt would otherwise render.

**Pass criteria**

- [ ] `npx tsc --noEmit` → exit 0.
- [ ] `npm run test` → 0 failures, **82 test files**, total up again.
- [ ] **The SFCC-863 suite passes unmodified.** `git diff` on `_app/index.test.tsx` must show only added lines in the mock block plus one added test. If either existing DNT assertion was edited, weakened or deleted, **stop** — that is the regression this PR is most likely to cause and the hardest to spot in review.
- [ ] The SFCC-885 drawer-breakpoint suite (4 tests) also passes unmodified.
- [ ] **New positive assertion in `_app/index.test.tsx`:** the language prompt mounts in the tree. Do it via a mock spy (same technique the file already uses for `drawerMenuSpy`), asserting the container received the expected `site`/`locale`/`buildUrl` props — not by rendering the real thing.
- [ ] `git diff -U0 overrides/app/components/_app/index.tsx` is **three lines or fewer** of real change. A larger diff means logic leaked into Tier 2 that belongs in the container.
- [ ] Container test asserts, each made to fail on purpose first: renders `null` when the predicate says no; renders the component when it says yes; **writes the cookie before assigning `window.location`** (assert ordering, not just that both happened — this is the whole reason the callback is synchronous); `onDismiss` writes the cookie and closes without navigating.
- [ ] `ZimmIcon` mocked in the container test.
- [ ] Any test touching `useMultiSite` mocks it with a factory — it ships untyped as `.js` with JSX from the base package and will not resolve otherwise.
- [ ] `npm run lint` → clean.
- [ ] `npm run audit:tokens` → still exactly **3**.

**Mandatory sub-step — prove the test can fail.** Especially the cookie-before-navigate ordering
assertion: an assertion that merely checks both calls occurred passes against the broken
implementation. It must be an ordering assertion and it must be demonstrated red against a
deliberately reversed implementation.

**Loop config**

| Agent | Weight | Brief |
|---|---|---|
| Tester | **Heavy** | Run `_app/index.test.tsx` in isolation first and confirm the SFCC-863 and SFCC-885 describes are green **before** looking at anything else. Then the container's own suite, including the reversed-order red run. |
| Scope-check | **Heavy** | Two Tier 2 files in this commit, both in `_app/`. Confirm the `_app/index.tsx` diff is ≤3 real lines and the `_app/index.test.tsx` diff is additive only. Confirm no fifth Tier 2 file appeared. |
| Scorer | PASS when | tsc clean **and** 82 files / 0 failures **and** DNT + SFCC-885 suites provably unmodified **and** the new mount assertion present **and** `_app/index.tsx` diff ≤3 lines **and** ordering assertion demonstrated red-then-green **and** lint clean **and** audit count 3. |

**Human handoff after this step.** The agent must **not** run `npm start`. Ask Marcel to verify on a
real EU domestic path with a non-matching browser language: the prompt appears, the CTA navigates to
the right site alias, the path is preserved, `refine` is dropped, and a reload inside the window does
not re-open it.

---

### Final gate — before opening the PR

Run in this order; all must pass:

1. `npx tsc --noEmit` → exit 0
2. `npm run lint` → clean
3. `npm run test` → **82 files, 0 failures**
4. `npm run audit:tokens` → **exactly 3** unacknowledged
5. `cr review --light --base develop` — required, not optional. Confirm `coderabbit auth status`
   first; if unauthenticated, `coderabbit auth login --api-key "$CODERABBIT_API_KEY"`. Advisory
   relative to the real merge gate, but it must actually run.

**PR body must contain, explicitly:**

- Which changes serve the stories and which are **incidental defect fixes with named beneficiaries**:
  - `prompt` size → **SFCC-831 only**
  - `minWidth` floor → **`zimmWishlistAuthDrawer` + Find in Boutique**; satisfies none of SFCC-831's own ACs. Fixes a real 768px cliff (full-width → 192px at one pixel of resize) and the fact that `25%` only delivers the designed 402px at a 1608px viewport, so every real laptop is under-width today.
  - `useUiCopy` close label → **all four drawer consumers** (`zimmPdpDrawer`, `zimmWishlistAuthDrawer`, the PDP boutique drawer, and this one).

- Why a new global modal in `_app` does not violate the SFCC-863 regression suite, and why
  `_app/index.test.tsx` had to change (the `ZimmIcon` module-eval throw, not a rendering change).

| # | Question | Owner / action |
|---|---|---|

REG-019 and SFCC-817 AC5 agree with each other; the 7-day window, added later in SFCC-823's comment thread, is the outlier. Still Emma's open item. | Emma Kirwan. Shipped as a named constant so a change is one line. |

## Unverified gaps in this plan

- The planner did not open the Figma nodes itself; every design value above is carried from the

  and the count strictly increasing**, not the exact integer.

content.text:
## The shape: three phases, and the order isn't negotiable

**Each phase can't start until the one before it exists.**

```
A. The drawer        →  B. The component      →  C. The trigger
   (adds a new size)     (uses that size)         (uses that component)
```

Phase B calls `<ZimmDrawer size="prompt">`. That size doesn't exist until A lands. Phase C renders the component B builds. So it's a chain, not a preference.

The one exception: **C1's three helpers depend on nothing.** Pure functions taking arguments and returning values — no component, no drawer. They could be written first, last, or in parallel.

**Eight commits, not one.** Not neatness — the split is doing a job. A1 adds the new size (serves our story). A2 fixes the English "Close" button (serves four unrelated drawers). Separating them means a reviewer reading `git log` can see which changes are ours and which are incidental fixes, **without being told.** That's the framing a separate PR would have given, for free.

---

## Step 0 — install

**What goes wrong without it:** you get failures that have nothing to do with our work and waste an hour chasing them.

**Why:** the Adyen merge landed on `develop` after your branch was cut, and it changed `package.json` plus ~1,564 lines of lockfile. Your `node_modules` may not match.

The planner checked and thinks it's probably already fine — but running it costs seconds and the alternative costs an afternoon. There's a check built in: `git status` must stay clean afterwards. If `npm install` *dirties* the lockfile, something's wrong with the dependency tree and we stop.

---

## Phase A — the shared drawer

### A1: the new size and the width floor

**Two separate things in one commit, because they're the same file and the same idea.**

**The floor** fixes something broken today. `small` is `25%` of the screen. On a tablet that's 208px holding content designed at 342px, so the button labels get cut off mid-word — the design itself specifies `nowrap` + `overflow: clip`, so there's no graceful failure. Adding `minWidth: 402px` means "never narrower than the design needs." It can only ever make a panel wider, so the two existing users of `small` can't regress.

**The `prompt` size** is new, for us only. On mobile our panel is content-height (434px) where the shell gives a near-full-height 898px. Rather than change the shared behaviour — which is PO-approved for the PDP drawer — we add an opt-in size nobody else uses.

**Three things in the pass criteria worth understanding:**

**The audit must say exactly 3.** Not 0, not 4. Three is the pre-existing violation count. Four means we introduced a raw value without the comment that marks it deliberate. **Zero means the audit didn't actually run** — and a check that silently doesn't run is worse than no check.

**The `parts` array must be byte-identical.** If it changed, a part was added by accident. An undeclared part keeps its base styling but silently loses its *variant* styling — so it breaks on exactly one variant and nothing reports it.

**Test files go 76 → 77.** We're adding one. If the count doesn't move, the new test file isn't being picked up.

**And the mandatory bit:** every new assertion has to be **made to fail on purpose first.** For a test that reads a plain object, this matters more than usual — such a test will happily pass against a recipe nobody changed. Four assertion groups, four inversions, four captured reds.

### A2: the English "Close" button

**What's wrong:** that label becomes the button's `aria-label`. An Italian screen-reader user on `/it-eu/` hears "Close" in English, inside a panel built specifically to speak their language. That's an accessibility defect, not polish.

**Why it's nearly free:** `useUiCopy` falls back to its inline English string when there's no provider. So no test, no story, nothing needs new setup. If a suite suddenly *does* need a wrapper, the hook was called in the wrong place — that's the check.

Fixes all four drawers at once.

---

## Phase B — the component

### B1: the prompt itself

**The core design decision: the component knows nothing.**

It takes a `variant` prop, looks up a row in a config table, and renders. No `if (variant === 'language')` anywhere in the JSX. That's the `zimmProductCard` pattern — adding a third variant later means adding a table row, not editing markup.

**And it never interprets its own callbacks.** The consumer passes a target identifier; the component hands it straight back untouched. It doesn't know what a site is, what a locale is, or what an alias is. That's what makes it reusable — and it satisfies the acceptance criterion that says the callback fires "with the target locale," without the component needing to understand what one is.

**Two silent-failure traps the criteria guard against:**

**Registration is two halves.** The recipe needs an import *and* a key in the exported object. Miss either and Chakra resolves the styles to `{}` — the component renders completely unstyled, with **no error at all.**

**The recipe key must start with `Zimm`.** Chakra's `extendTheme` deep-merges. A recipe called `Footer` silently inherits Salesforce's `Footer` styling rather than replacing it. The prefix is what stops that.

**On states:** Figma defines only a default state — no hover, focus, disabled, loading, error. That's a confirmed absence, not something we failed to find. So the component authors **no** state styling of its own; the buttons are real `<button>` elements inheriting all of it from `ZimmButton`. Two styling surfaces for one interactive component is how they drift apart.

### B2: the Contentful seed script

**What goes wrong without it:** the Italian storefront shows English, forever, and nothing tells you.

**Why:** every non-default Contentful locale falls back to English. A missing Italian translation doesn't error and doesn't show a broken key — it quietly serves English. For a feature whose entire purpose is showing the message in the storefront's own language, that's the requirement failing invisibly.

**The fix:** seed the eight keys with English values now. The gap becomes *visible* — eight entries sitting in the CMS with no Italian value, where the content team actually works, instead of hidden behind a fallback.

One detail that matters: **store sentence case, not capitals.** The CSS uppercases it. Hand a translator SHOUTING TEXT and you get shouting text back, in a language with different capitalisation rules.

---

## Phase C — the trigger

### C1: three pure functions

**No component, no drawer, no browser needed. Just inputs and outputs.**

**The cookie module** has one unusual requirement: its parsing must work **without a browser.** The client writes the cookie, but next sprint the *server* will read it from the request header to decide whether to redirect. If parsing is tangled up with `document`, the server can't reuse it, and someone re-implements it — and then there are two parsers that drift.

Also: `try/catch` on **read as well as write**. Safari private mode throws when you *read* storage, not just when you write. That's documented in this codebase already, from a bug someone else hit.

**The URL builder** handles: shopper is on `/it-eu/products/silk-dress`, wants French, should land on `/fr-eu/products/silk-dress` — same product, not the homepage. The base template has a helper that almost does this, but it swaps the locale *within* a site, and our four EU languages are separate sites.

**The predicate** answers one question: should the prompt show? Six inputs in, a yes/no and a target out. Because it's pure, all six scenarios are testable in milliseconds with no browser.

**The check that keeps us honest:** zero `js-cookie` imports. That library is on disk, but only because another package depends on it — it's not ours. Using it means depending on something we never declared, which breaks the day that package drops it.

### C2: the broken hook

**This step is the clearest illustration of why fail-on-purpose is mandatory.**

`useCountryConfig` returns the **Australian** config on all four EU storefronts. It compares the config's SFCC ID (`ZimmermannEU`) against the runtime's site ID (`ZimmermannEUfr`). Those never match, so it falls through to the default.

**It has a test suite. The suite passes. It has passed for months.** Because the test mocks the site ID as `'ZimmermannEU'` — a value the real config **can never produce.** The test asserts against a fiction.

So the order here is strict: **write the failing test first, watch it go red against the current code, then fix.** A green run on this file has already proven nothing once; we're not accepting another one.

It's a one-line fix. The discipline around it is the point.

### C3: mounting it — the sharpest review point

**This is where the PR is most likely to go wrong, and the plan is heaviest here.**

The prompt fires on every EU page, so it mounts in `_app` — the shell that wraps every route. That's a Tier 2 file, and the plan caps the change at **three lines or fewer.** A bigger diff means logic leaked into the shell that belongs in the container.

**The trap:** `_app/index.test.tsx` exists *specifically* to assert that a global modal never renders again. Salesforce shipped an unconfigurable placeholder modal, SFCC-863 ripped it out, and left a regression suite to keep it out. We're now adding a different global modal.

**And that test file has to change** — for a reason that has nothing to do with our modal. `ZimmButton` imports `ZimmIcon`, which imports Salesforce's icon barrel, which crashes under the test runner **when the module loads**, not when anything renders. So the moment `_app` imports anything reaching the drawer, that suite dies on import, before a single assertion runs.

So the fix is one mock. But the risk is real: a builder hitting an unexplained red suite next to those DNT assertions might "fix" it by weakening them — the exact regression they exist to prevent. The plan makes it a hard scope-check: **the diff must be additive only.** If an existing assertion was edited, stop.

**And one subtle test requirement:** the cookie must be written *before* the page navigates away. A test asserting "both things happened" passes against a broken implementation — the page unloads and the cookie write is lost, but both functions were called. So it has to be an **ordering** assertion, proven red against a deliberately reversed implementation.

---

## The final gate

Five checks, in order: types, lint, tests (82 files, zero failures), the token audit (exactly 3), and a local CodeRabbit review. That last one is required by the project rules, not optional — advisory relative to the real PR review, but it has to actually run.

---

## Two places the loop stops and asks you

**Nothing automated can prove a rendered width.** In the test environment every element reports a size of zero. So after A1 you look at the drawer at three screen sizes to confirm the floor made it wider, not narrower. And after C3 you check the real journey — prompt appears, CTA goes to the right place, path preserved, reload doesn't re-open it.

The agent will never run `npm start`. It asks you.

---

## What makes this a plan rather than a task list

Three things:

**Every pass criterion is a command with an expected output.** Not "tests pass" — "77 files, zero failures, audit says exactly 3." Checkable by someone who wasn't in this conversation.

**The fail-on-purpose requirement runs throughout.** A test that has never been observed failing hasn't been shown to test anything. `useCountryConfig` is the proof.

**The dangerous steps are named as dangerous.** C3 gets heavy scope-checking because it's Tier 2 next to a regression suite. A1 gets four separate red-run proofs because object-reading tests pass too easily. The effort is concentrated where it's actually needed rather than spread evenly.

content.text:
## 1. The one decision everything else hangs on

### Browser language, not geo-IP

**What it decided:** whether SFCC-689 is a day's work or blocked until October.

**The situation:** three sources, two answers. The ticket's acceptance criteria said *browser language*. REG-029 — a Confirmed requirement — said *GEO-IP detected country*. The approved Figma copy said *"we noticed you are in France"*, which is a location, backing REG-029.

**Why it mattered so much:** geo-IP doesn't exist anywhere in this codebase. The file where it would live is still Salesforce's untouched example stub. Building it is SFCC-817 — **Sprint 6, and still only In Refinement.** So "geo-IP" meant 689 couldn't be finished this sprint at all. "Browser language" meant it needs nothing that doesn't already exist.

**The evidence that tipped it:** the board was re-planned overnight. SFCC-823 and SFCC-817 both moved to Sprint 6. **SFCC-689 stayed in Sprint 5, alone.** That split only makes sense if 689 isn't supposed to need IP detection — otherwise it would have moved with them.

**The cost you're carrying:** it diverges from a Confirmed requirement, so it has to be recorded as a deliberate override. Otherwise UAT tests against REG-029 and fails work that's correctly built.

**The bonus nobody planned:** browser language is one line to fake in a test (`test.use({ locale: 'fr-FR' })`). Faking an IP address in CI needs a proxy. **The decision made the feature testable as a side effect.**

---

## 2. Decisions that stopped us shipping a defect

### The cookie must be set at `path=/`

**Without it:** the shopper taps "view in French", lands on the French site, and the prompt fires again. Immediately. Every time. An infinite loop on the *happy path*.

**Why:** cookies are tied to a path by default. All ten storefronts are folders on one website — `/it-eu/`, `/fr-eu/` — so a cookie written on the Italian path is invisible on the French one. And our redirect *is* a path change.

### `SameSite=Lax`

**Without it:** a shopper arriving from Instagram or Google Shopping gets prompted again despite having dismissed it — and only from those entry points, which makes it look random and nearly impossible to reproduce.

**Why:** browsers won't send `Strict` cookies when you arrive from another site. REG-035 names Instagram and Google Shopping explicitly. It's the requirement's own list that would break.

### A dismiss callback on every close path

**Without it:** the shopper closes the panel with the X, and nothing gets recorded — so the prompt returns on the next page.

**Why:** the acceptance criteria only named a callback for one of the four ways to close it. The consumer has to write the cookie when the shopper "dismisses **or** acts on" it, so it needs a hook on all four.

**Your 09-09 run caught this.** It was still open when we picked it up.

### Tokens that carry phrases, not nouns

**Without it:** the Italian copy reads wrong. Not slightly — visibly, like machine translation.

**Why:** French, Italian and Spanish inflect. "in Francia", "dell'Italia", "degli Emirati" — the preposition changes with the word. A `{country}` slot can't carry that. **The design already demonstrates the failure twice**: one button reads "PASSA AL NEGOZIO SAN MARINO" while its own body text correctly says "al negozio **di** San Marino", and another reads "SHIPSPEDISCI" — an English and an Italian template fused.

**The fix costs nothing:** name the token `{inCountry}` instead of `{country}`. Identical in English. Lets the copy author supply "in Francia" — preposition included — without anyone touching code.

---

## 3. Decisions that kept us unblocked

### Ship derived fallbacks instead of waiting for copy

**The alternative:** wait for the BA. Which could be days.

**What we noticed:** the design's *sentences* are recoverable — only the example values were incoherent (it says "you're in the UK" then "you're shopping on the UK store", which can't both be true or there'd be no mismatch). And one of them, the language body, matches REG-031's prescribed format word for word.

**So:** write the English fallbacks into the code now. The component works today. Real copy arrives later as a Contentful edit — **no code change, no deploy.**

**Plus the seed script**, because an un-authored Italian translation renders in English *silently*. Seeding eight keys makes the gap visible in the CMS instead of hidden behind a fallback.

### Spec only what's specified — no third cookie flag

**The temptation:** I'd designed a third flag for "shopper made a manual selection", because SFCC-817 promises to honour one.

**What the evidence said:** nothing specifies storing it. REG-024 says the selection persists *as the URL* — you're on `/fr-eu/`, that **is** the record. SFCC-688 has eight acceptance criteria and none mentions saving anything.

**So SFCC-817 is promising to honour something no story writes.** That's 817's problem, not ours, and it's in refinement right now — the right moment to raise it.

**We cut the flag.** A version prefix on the cookie means adding it later strands nothing.

---

## 4. Decisions about touching shared code

### The width floor goes on the *existing* size

**Why this was delicate:** `small` is used by the wishlist login panel and Find in Boutique. Change it wrong and you break two shipped features.

**Three options were on the table.** Pin it to a fixed 402px — but that makes both existing panels *narrower* on large monitors. Add a brand-new size just for us — safe, but leaves both of them with the bug we just proved. Or add a floor.

**The floor wins because it's monotonic: it can only ever make a panel wider, never narrower.** No existing consumer can regress. And it fixes a cliff at exactly 768px where the panel collapses from full-width to 192px on one pixel of resize — for all three consumers, not just ours.

### The mobile height gets a *new* size

**Opposite call, and the reason matters.**

The width was a **defect** — the shell couldn't deliver what its own design needs. The mobile height is **not a defect**: the shell's own design says 898px tall and the code implements exactly that, and the 58px strip is separately PO-approved for the PDP drawer.

Our banner wants something different. That's a *missing option*, not a bug. So: a new opt-in size that nobody else uses, rather than changing behaviour that's correct for everyone else.

**Same file, opposite treatment, because the problems are different kinds.**

### Fixing the English "Close" button

**Scope creep, deliberately accepted.** It's a shared atom, in a story about a banner.

**Why it earned its place:** that label is what a screen reader announces. An Italian user hears "Close" in English inside a panel built to speak their language. And the fix repairs all four drawers at once, in a file we're already opening.

---

## 5. Where you overruled me — and were right both times

### The width floor

I called for a fixed 402px. You said: use a minimum, and let it grow.

**You were right, for a reason I'd underweighted** — `small` has two live consumers, and my version would have shrunk both on large screens. Yours can only widen. For a shared component, that's a much safer shape.

### The precedence rule

I'd worked up a rule about the country prompt suppressing the language prompt, and talked about adding an input to 689's trigger.

**You asked: if the collision is designed out, why change anything?** And you were right — the check belongs to SFCC-823, which is the one that knows about country mismatches. 689 stays ignorant, which is exactly why it needs no geo-IP. I'd muddied my own position.

### Three smaller corrections the process caught

- I said the buttons were 52px. They're **responsive** — 52px desktop, 40px mobile. Different prop.
- I said tablet needed ~50% width. The tablet content symbol is **byte-identical to desktop** — I'd measured a frame, not the content.
- I said REG-030 was **unsatisfiable** from browser language. It isn't — the five countries collapse onto three languages, which is exactly what browser language gives us.

---

## 6. The process decisions

**One branch, one PR, both stories.** 689 is unbuildable without 831, and 831 has no consumer without 689. Splitting them ships dead code in one PR and an unreviewable diff in the other.

**The cost:** the drawer fixes serve components that have nothing to do with these stories. With no separate PR to isolate them, **the PR body has to say so explicitly** — which changes serve the stories, which are incidental fixes, and who benefits. That's the framing a split would have given, for free.

**Jira after the build, not before.** Your call: build, test, confirm, *then* document — so the record reflects what actually shipped rather than what we planned.

**The one thing that gets riskier by waiting:** the REG-029 override. If it isn't on the ticket before UAT looks at it, correctly-built work fails against a requirement we knowingly diverged from. Everything else on the list can wait; that one is cheap now and annoying later.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/.claude/skills/zimmerMANNBuild

The executor. Takes an approved plan and builds it, one step at a time, with every step tested,
scope-checked, scored and seen by Marcel before it becomes a commit.

**Intended model: Sonnet 5 at maximum effort.** A skill cannot pin the session model — the loop
agents are pinned to Sonnet in their own frontmatter regardless.

**Scale to the work.** A two-point story does not get the full loop. The plan states the scale it
chose and why; honour it. Over-scaled machinery is a defect, not thoroughness. Nothing too crazy,
no overthinking.

**Report in "ELI5BITFEDLOTP" register** — Explain Like I'm 5, But I'm The FED Lead Of The
Project. Not dumbed down, but no jargon that gets in the way: lead with the consequence, then the
mechanism, then the fix. This is the default for everything you put in front of Marcel unless he
asks for a different level.

---

## Two modes

**`build`** — `` is a Jira key. Reads `~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills/.runs/<TICKET>/plan.md`
and executes it. This is the default.

**`rework`** — invoked as `rework <TICKET>` after a PR is open and CodeRabbit or a reviewer has
requested changes. Skips planning entirely; see the last section.

If no plan exists for the ticket, stop and say so. **Do not plan here** — that is
`zimmerMANNPreBuild`'s job, and building from an unplanned story is how an afternoon gets burned
on the wrong thing.

---

## Before the first step

1. Confirm the branch. **Not `develop`, not `main`** — a `PreToolUse` hook blocks every Write and
   Edit there. If the branch is wrong, stop.
2. Confirm the working tree is clean, or that everything dirty is expected and belongs to this
   story. Registry churn under `.claude/registry/*.md` is automatic and expected.
3. Read the plan's file manifest, tiers and per-step pass criteria. **Any file marked BLOCKED
   stops the run** until Marcel confirms owner approval.
4. Record the baseline: run the four per-step gates now and note the numbers. A gate that is
   non-zero at baseline is not a failure you introduced.

---

## The loop — once per step

```
Implementer  →  Tester  →  Orchestrator  →  Scorer  →  [Marcel]  →  commit
                   ↑                          │
                   └────── REWORK, max 3 ─────┘
```

**1. `zm-implementer`** builds the step. Only the files the step names. It never stages and never
commits.

**2. `zm-tester`** fans out its own angle sub-agents, re-pointed for this step, and reports
findings with CONFIRMED/PLAUSIBLE and UNIFORM/ONE-OFF labels, plus what it tried to falsify and
what it could not verify.

**3. `zm-orchestrator`** returns a scope verdict — IN SCOPE / UNDER / OVER / BLOCKED. Under and
over carry equal weight.

**4. `zm-scorer`** takes both and scores six axes. PASS or REWORK.

**REWORK returns to the Implementer with a specific instruction. Maximum three rounds.** On the
third, stop and surface to Marcel — three failures means the plan or the criteria are wrong, not
the implementation.

**A step prompt may narrow what an agent looks at. It may never contradict that agent's brief, and
it may never pre-answer the question the agent exists to ask.** Before dispatching, read the prompt
against the brief. If you are telling the Implementer not to stop and ask, telling the Orchestrator
which files to leave out of the manifest check, or handing the Tester a measurement to treat as
given, you have disabled the agent while still collecting its verdict. All three have happened: one
build's step prompts carried "do not stop and ask, do not leave a TODO" against a stop-and-ratify
rule added to `zm-implementer.md` days earlier, and another narrowed the Orchestrator's diff by
instruction, then relayed its "IN SCOPE, clean" onward — where PostBuild's own Orchestrator later
returned OVER on that same diff.

**If a narrowing is genuinely wanted, carry it into the verdict you relay.** "IN SCOPE, against a
manifest I restricted" is a usable answer. "IN SCOPE, clean" is not.

### Per-step gates — the cheap four

Run every step. Seconds each.

```
npx tsc --noEmit
npm run test                        # includes recipeGuards, the hard styling gate
npm run lint                        # compare counts, not the exit code
node scripts/auditTokenUsage.mjs    # new unacknowledged findings only
```

Two traps: `npm run lint` exits non-zero at a healthy baseline, so **compare the count against
your baseline and ignore the exit code**. And never append arguments to it — `pwa-kit-dev lint`
forwards `--`-args into `execSync`, which can silently turn the gate into a writer.

The plan's per-step pass criteria layer **on top of** these, they do not replace them.

### The visual checkpoint

**After any step that changes rendered output, the loop stops.** The plan marks which steps those
are; if it doesn't, assume any step touching a component, a recipe or a page does.

Tell Marcel exactly:
- the URL and the viewport to open
- the Figma node to compare against — the one for **that variant and state**
- what should be on screen
- what would indicate a defect, including anything that will look wrong but is correct

Then **wait.** Do not proceed on assumption. This is the only gate on this stack that catches a
layout defect — `width: 'xl'` passed every automated check and destroyed the global footer.

Until it has happened, the Scorer's Design fidelity axis is UNVERIFIED, not passed.

### The commit

**The skill commits, not an agent.** Only after: Scorer PASS, and the visual checkpoint passed if
one was owed.

**State the provenance in the commit turn, or do not commit.** Name the step, which loop agents
actually ran for it, the Scorer's verdict and round, and the visual checkpoint's outcome. Any of
those that did not happen is written as **"did not run"** in those words — and a commit carrying
`did not run` against the Scorer, or against an owed visual checkpoint, stops for Marcel's
explicit override instead of proceeding. The loop collapsing into one inline agent is the most
expensive failure this skill has: it is invisible from inside, and re-reading this file mid-build
does not restore it. Only a per-commit statement makes it visible while it is still happening.

One step, one commit. Conventional Commits — the `commit-msg` hook enforces it. **No Claude
attribution, no CodeRabbit mentions, no `Co-Authored-By` line.** Use Marcel's previously authored
commits on this repo as the reference for tone and body.

Then move to the next step.

---

## Before handing off

Once every step has passed, run the expensive gates **once**:

```
npm run build-storybook             # then run the interaction + a11y suite against it
npm run test:story                  # real BrowserStack, scoped to the Jira key
npm run test:max-file-size          # runs a full build
cr review --base develop            # CodeRabbit locally, full review before anything is public
```

Storybook needs a verified-free port and a build you can prove is yours — a stale server on 6006
produced a silently meaningless pass once. Check the served build matches your own before trusting
any result.

Then **write the handoff** to `~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills/.runs/<TICKET>/handoff.md`:

```
# Handoff — <TICKET>
Branch: <branch>   Base: <sha>   Head: <sha>

## Steps
| # | What | Commit | Scorer verdict | Rework rounds |

## Gates (real numbers, not claims)
| Gate | Result | Baseline |

## UNIFORM findings
<each one, with file:line — these are what a per-step review structurally cannot catch>

## Could not verify
<named, with why>

## Outstanding
<anything left, or "none">
```

**Write it even when everything passed** — and do not wait until here to start it. Create the file
at the first commit and append its Steps row on every commit thereafter, so it exists even when a
build never formally reaches this section. PostBuild reads this file, and it may run in a
different session — a handoff that exists only in conversation does not survive the session
ending.

This is not hypothetical: `handoff.md` exists for one story in ten. The trigger above is
unreachable in exactly the builds that most need it, because it sits behind "once every step has
passed" and a collapsed loop never passes a step. Its absence is not neutral — PostBuild infers
from a missing handoff that the loop never ran, and wrote exactly that into a durable artefact for
a build whose Scorer verdicts were recoverable from the subagent transcripts all along.

Then present the same content to Marcel and **hand off to `zimmerMANNPostBuild`. This skill does
not push and does not open a PR.**

---

## Rework mode

Entered after a PR is open and CodeRabbit or a reviewer has requested changes.

**Read `~/Dev/zimmerMANN-skills/.runs/<TICKET>/postbuild.md` first.** It records what earlier rounds
already declined and why. A finding that was declined with evidence in round one does not get
re-litigated in round three — check before you verify anything, and if you disagree with a previous
decline, say so rather than silently reversing it.

**1. Verify every finding before touching anything.** CodeRabbit has been wrong on this repo
often — one batch ran 1-in-6 correct. Treat each finding as a hypothesis, not a fact. Per finding:

- **VALID** — reproduce it, cite `file:line`, fix it
- **INVALID** — say what is actually true, with the evidence, and draft the reply
- **OUT OF SCOPE** — real but not this story's problem; name the owning ticket or the person
- **DEFER** — real, in scope, but blocked on a decision; name who decides

**2. Fix only the VALID ones.** Same rules as build mode — the Implementer touches only what the
finding names, never stages, never commits.

**3. Re-run the cheap four**, plus the visual checkpoint if the fix changes rendered output.

**4. Commit the fixes here**, same rule as build mode — the skill commits, never an agent. Reference
the review thread each commit answers.

**5. Hand back to `zimmerMANNPostBuild`** with: what was fixed and in which commit, what was
declined and why, and the evidence behind each decline. **PostBuild owns the push and the
in-thread replies** — every finding gets a written answer, including the declined ones.

---

## Hard rules

- **Never push. Never open or update a PR.** That boundary belongs to PostBuild, which presents
  first and pushes only once Marcel has given the go.
- **Never write to the repo's config** — `.claude/**`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `CODEOWNERS`,
  `.docs/memory/**`, `.docs/prd/**`. Tier 1 Governance.
- **Never touch a Tier 1 file** without Marcel naming it and confirming owner approval.
- **Never expand scope.** Something worth doing that the plan didn't ask for gets reported, not
  done. Report it and let Marcel decide.
- **Local-only docs are never citable** in a commit message or a code comment. Cite `AGENTS.md`
  or `.claude/rules/*` instead.
- **Say what you could not verify.** Silence reads as "nothing wrong" when it may mean
  "didn't look there".

---

## What Marcel is missing

Close every report with this section. Always, even when it is one line.

This is **not** "what I could not verify" — that is your own blind spot and it has its own home.
This is his: something he has not thought to ask about, a decision he is about to make on a stale
premise, a risk sitting just outside this task that you can see from where you are standing, or a

## Report — Step A1: `ZimmDrawer` prompt size + narrow-panel width floor

**What breaks today, and what this fixes:** the `small` drawer (Find in Boutique, and soon the SFCC-831 language prompt) only reaches its *designed* 402px width on a 1608px-wide screen, because its old `25%` cap only equals 402px at that one viewport — every real laptop renders it narrower than intended. This step adds a fixed 402px floor so the panel never goes below its designed width, and adds a new `prompt` drawer size (auto-height, content-sized, capped and scrollable) that SFCC-831's mismatch banner will use next.

**Files changed — exactly the four named, nothing else:**

1. `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/overrides/app/components/ui-kits/atoms/zimmDrawer/zimmDrawer.css.ts`
   - Added `PANEL_MIN_NARROW = '25.125rem'` (line 37) with `// audit-allow: provisional — pending a --zimm-* foundation token`, matching `zimmButton.css.ts:244`'s exact vocabulary.
   - Added shared `NARROW_WIDTH_ABOVE_MD = { width: WIDTH_SMALL, minWidth: PANEL_MIN_NARROW, maxWidth: '100%' }` (line 43), same technique as `INSET_COMPACT`/`INSET_LARGE`.
   - Rewrote `small`'s `@media (min-width: md)` block to spread `NARROW_WIDTH_ABOVE_MD` instead of its old `width/maxWidth: WIDTH_SMALL` pair — `maxWidth` is now `'100%'`, not `'25%'`.
   - Added the new `prompt` variant: `height: 'auto'` / `maxHeight: calc(100% - MOBILE_BOTTOM_GAP)` / `overflowY: 'auto'` at base, `...NARROW_WIDTH_ABOVE_MD` + `height: '100%'` + `maxHeight: '100%'` above `md`.
   - `parts` array (line 72) untouched — confirmed by diff and by a test assertion.

2. `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/overrides/app/components/ui-kits/atoms/zimmDrawer/index.tsx`
   - Single line changed (line 37): `ZimmDrawerSize` union gained `| 'prompt'`. Nothing else in this file touched, per the manifest's explicit restriction.

3. `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/overrides/app/components/ui-kits/atoms/zimmDrawer/index.stories.tsx`
   - Added `Prompt` story (4 lines), same shape as `XLarge` — bare `render`, no `play`.

4. `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/overrides/app/components/ui-kits/atoms/zimmDrawer/zimmDrawer.css.test.ts` — **new file**, 6 tests, asserting exactly the four things the plan named: `small`+`prompt` both emit `minWidth: '25.125rem'` above `md`; `prompt` emits `height: 'auto'`/the `calc()` `maxHeight` at base and `'100%'`/`'100%'` above `md`; `small` no longer emits `maxWidth: '25%'`; plus a `parts`-array regression guard.

**Evidence per pass criterion:**
- `npx tsc --noEmit` → exit 0, no output (checked twice, before and after the fail-on-purpose cycle).
- `npm run test` → **77 test files** (was 76), **1170 tests** (was 1164, threshold was `>1164`), **0 failures**.
- `npm run test -- recipeGuards` → 6/6 green in isolation.
- `npm run audit:tokens` → **"3 unacknowledged violation(s) found."** — unchanged from baseline; the new `PANEL_MIN_NARROW` appears correctly in the *acknowledged* list at `zimmDrawer.css.ts:37`.
- `parts` array byte-identical — confirmed by `git diff` and by the new test's own assertion.
- Ripple spot-check: `grep -rn "Record<ZimmDrawerSize" overrides/` → no matches anywhere, and `zimmPdpDrawer/index.tsx:36-51` confirms `size` is passed straight through to `useMultiStyleConfig`/`<ZimmDrawer size={size}>` — widening the union cannot break exhaustiveness.
- Fail-on-purpose: inverted all four assertion groups at once, ran the suite (captured 5/6 red, each failure showing the correct vs. inverted value — pasted above), reverted via a scratchpad backup, confirmed byte-identical revert via `diff`, re-ran (6/6 green).
- One of my own test assertions was itself wrong on the first pass (`toContain('25%')` incorrectly flagged the untouched `width: '25%'`) — caught by the real run, fixed to check `maxWidth` specifically, not touched the recipe.
- `git status`/`git diff --cached --stat` confirm nothing staged, nothing outside the four named files touched (the `.claude/registry/*.md` and translation JSON diffs were already dirty before I started, per the session's opening `git status` snapshot — not mine).

**Noticed, not touched (per instruction):**
- `index.tsx`'s docblock immediately above `ZimmDrawerSize` (lines ~34–36) says "Matches Figma's own named drawer sizes exactly (SFCC-898)" and lists five sizes — now stale, since `prompt` is a sixth size that isn't part of that original five-name table. Left untouched, as instructed.
- The plan's own spot-check citation for the ripple check (`zimmTabs/index.tsx:48`) doesn't exist at that path — `zimmTabs/` only contains `zimmTabs.css.ts` (a recipe file, no component). I verified the underlying safety claim a different way (the `Record<ZimmDrawerSize, ...>` grep + `zimmPdpDrawer`'s passthrough), which holds, but flagging the stale citation since I was told never to assert a file:line without checking it.

## What Marcel is missing

Nothing new this pass beyond what plan.md's own "What Marcel is missing" already names (the zero-E2E-coverage gap for the whole SFCC-831/689 feature) — that's a Tier 1 CI-config problem out of this step's reach, not something A1 changes. Worth flagging locally: the `prompt` variant's real 402px-floor-plus-content-height behaviour is exactly the kind of thing jsdom can't prove (every rect reports 0), so the plan's own human-checkpoint after this step — checking `size="small"` on Find in Boutique at ~1440/834/390px — is doing real work here, not a formality; nothing in this loop can substitute for it.</result>
